The Handoff Protocol

# The Handoff Protocol

## What survives a session boundary, and with what authority

*Deployed as `docs/governance/protocols/handoff.md`. Works with `docs/governance/protocols/root-cause.md`, `docs/governance/protocols/correction-loop.md` and `docs/governance/protocols/descent.md`.*

## Purpose

Every other protocol governs work inside a session. None governs what
crosses the boundary when the session ends.

What crosses is a summary, and a summary is where the information
that mattered most gets lost — not the facts, which survive, but the
*status* of the facts. Which claims were established and which
were guesses. Which decisions a person made and which an agent proposed
and nobody objected to. What was tried and rejected. Why the work
stopped.

Four failures follow, and all four are churn:

**Re-diagnosis.** The next agent re-probes candidates
the last one already rejected, because the rejections were in a context
window that no longer exists. The work is repeated at full cost and the
repetition is invisible — it looks like diligence.

**Provenance collapse.** "We decided to use the registry
proxy" reads identically whether a person decided it, an agent suggested
it and got a shrug, or it was one option in a list nobody picked. A
summary flattens all three into the same sentence, and the next session
inherits a decision that was never made.

**Silent incompleteness.** *Built, tested* is a
true and complete-sounding report that omits *nothing calls it*.
The handoff records what was done, and what was not done leaves no
trace, because an absence has no author.

**Stale authority.** A handoff written six weeks ago
describes a tree that has changed. Read as current, it sends the next
agent to fix something already fixed, or to build on a decision since
reversed.

**A handoff is context, not authority.** It tells the
next session what happened. It never tells them what they are permitted
to skip.

That sentence is the protocol; the rest is machinery for making it
hold, because the natural reading of an inherited note is the opposite —
a prior session's work feels like a foundation rather than a report, and
*the last agent established the cause* feels like a reason not to
establish it again.

**Scope.** Any point where work passes between contexts:
session end, agent handoff, a fleet worker's run boundary, an
orchestrator delegating, a person picking up an item someone else
started. Not only long gaps — a compaction inside one long run crosses
the same boundary and loses the same things.

**What it guarantees.** That the next reader can tell an
established fact from a proposal, that the handoff's claims can be
checked against the tree rather than believed, and that nothing in it
grants an exemption.

**What it does not guarantee.** That the handoff is
complete or that the previous session was right. It makes both checkable
rather than assumed.

## Context, not authority

The distinction is everything, and it is not intuitive. A handoff
arrives as a document from someone who knew more about this item than
you do, written by a session that did the work. Every instinct treats it
as a foundation.

It is a report. Reports are read, weighed and checked. Foundations
are built on without looking.

| A handoff may | A handoff may never |

| Say what was observed, with its evidence | Assert a cause that has no diagnosis artifact |

| Say what was decided, and by whom | Turn a proposal into a decision by describing it as one |

| Say what was tried and rejected, with the probe output | Save the next session from re-probing something never actually probed |

| Name the state the work was left in | Be the source of truth for that state |

| Record an open question | Instruct the next session to answer it |

| Point at artifacts | Substitute for them |

### The two failures this prevents

**Inherited exemption.** "The previous session
established the cause" is not a diagnosis artifact, and a session that
proceeds to a fix on the strength of that sentence has skipped step 2 of
the Correction Loop while believing it did not. Section 7 states this in
full because it is the failure most likely to happen and the hardest to
see afterwards — the fix looks properly grounded, and the grounding is a
sentence in a note.

**Inherited agenda.** An open question in a handoff —
*should we also fix the retry logic?* — is a record that someone
wondered. It is not a task, not a commitment, and not permission to
descend. The next session reads it, notes it, and does the work it was
assigned. If the question matters it becomes an item through intake,
like everything else.

This matters more than it sounds because open questions are the part
of a handoff most likely to be acted on. They read as the unfinished
business the writer wanted picked up, and picking them up is how one
session's speculation becomes three sessions of unplanned work.

### The reading stance

A session reading a handoff assumes:

- It was true when written. Not that it is true now — see section 6.

- It is incomplete. What is absent was not necessarily considered; silence is not a negative finding.

- It carries no permissions. Every gate that applies to this item still applies.

- Its claims are checkable. Where the handoff and the tree disagree, the tree wins — see section 5.

None of that means treating the handoff as untrustworthy. It is
usually accurate and it is usually the fastest route into an item. The
stance is the one you would take toward a colleague's careful notes from
six weeks ago: valuable, worth reading first, and not a substitute for
looking.

## Provenance tagging

Every line in a handoff carries a tag. Untagged prose is not a
handoff, it is a note.

| Tag | Means | Next session may |

| `[decided]` | A person chose this, or a gate enforced it | Rely on it; changing it is a decision of its own |

| `[proposed]` | An agent suggested it; nobody ratified it | Reconsider freely. Not a commitment |

| `[observed]` | Measured, with the command and output recorded | Rely on it as of the timestamp; re-run if the tree moved |

| `[assumed]` | Believed without checking, and the writer knew it | Verify before relying. This is the highest-value tag |

### Why four and not two

The collapse this prevents is specifically between
`[decided]` and `[proposed]`. An agent proposes an
approach, the operator says "sounds good" or says nothing, and by the
time it reaches a summary it is *we decided*. Six weeks later
nobody can distinguish a considered choice from an unopposed suggestion,
and the unopposed suggestion has the same force.

The test is mechanical: **did a person state it, or did an agent state it and no one object?** Acquiescence is
`[proposed]`. It may be right, it may be what everyone wants,
and it is still not a decision until someone makes one.

`[assumed]` earns its place by being the tag nobody wants
to write. An agent that believed the runner was present without
checking, and says so, has given the next session the single most useful
line in the handoff. A protocol with no honest way to record an
unchecked belief gets handoffs where everything reads as
`[observed]`.

### What tagging looks like

```
## FIND-4412 — test-gate skips on JS changes

- [observed] 8 of 8 skipped changesets classified as rust by detectEcosystem
(scripts/diagnosis/census.mjs, 2026-09-21T14:02Z)
- [decided] Fix at the detector, not at the gate — operator, 2026-09-21
- [proposed] Also add a skip-reason field to the stage stream. Not ratified
- [assumed] The base checkout is fine; never probed
- [observed] Diagnosis artifact at docs/diagnosis/FIND-4412.json, verdict CORRELATE-ONLY
```

Five lines, and a reader knows exactly how much weight each carries.
The same five lines written as prose would read as a coherent account in
which everything is equally true.

### The tags are about origin, not confidence

Origin is checkable; confidence is not. An agent very sure of
something it never measured writes `[assumed]`, not
`[observed]`. An agent doubtful about a measured result still
writes `[observed]` and puts the doubt in the line.

This is the same distinction the Root Cause Protocol makes with
`not-probed`: the vocabulary has to let an agent say what it
actually did, or it will describe what it wishes it had done.

## Derived state, not narrated state

The agent writes the reasoning. The machine writes the state. This
split is what keeps a handoff from becoming a claim about a tree the
writer is no longer looking at.

### What the handoff generator derives

| Field | Source |

| Item, depth, parent, chain | Work record |

| Current stage and the last five stage events | Stage stream |

| Branch, head commit, files changed, diff size | git |

| Diagnosis artifact path and verdict | `docs/diagnosis/ .json` |

| Gate results at last run, including any exit 2 | CI |

| Captures opened during this session | Capture store |

| Open chains, and whether this session closed them | Chain record |

| Session wall clock, token spend, retries | Run telemetry |

None of this is typed by the agent, and none of it can be wrong in
the direction the agent wishes. *Built, tested* stops being a
possible summary when the generated block says the gate returned
`skip` and the orphan check lists a new entry.

**That is the fix for silent incompleteness.** The
absence has no author, so it needs a machine to notice it. A derived
block that prints `Caller: none` and
`Orphan baseline: +1` says the thing no narrative was going
to say.

### What the agent writes

Four things, all tagged, none of them state:

- Why the work stopped. Finished, blocked, out of budget, abandoned at depth 1, session ended. This is the single most useful line and it is the one most often missing — handoffs record where the work is, not why it is there.

- What was tried and rejected , with probe output. This is what prevents re-diagnosis, and it is worth more than the conclusions.

- What the next session should know that is not visible in the tree. A misleading name, a test that passes for the wrong reason, a dependency that looks unused and is not.

- Open questions , tagged and understood as records rather than instructions.

### The conclusion goes last and stays short

There is a strong pull toward opening a handoff with a confident
summary — *the problem is X, the fix is Y, next step is Z*.
Resist it. That paragraph is where all four provenance categories get
flattened back together, and it is the part the next session will read
instead of the tagged lines above it.

If a conclusion is warranted it is one tagged line like everything
else, and if it rests on a diagnosis artifact it cites the path rather
than restating the finding.

### Compaction is a handoff

When a long run compacts its context, the same rules apply. The
compacted summary is a handoff from the session to itself, it inherits
all four failures, and an agent reading its own compacted notes is in
exactly the position of an agent reading someone else's — the original
observations are gone and only the summary remains.

Generate the derived block at compaction and keep it. It costs almost
nothing and it is the difference between resuming and re-deriving.

## The resumption gate

Writing a good handoff is half the protocol. The other half is what
the next session does before acting on it, and it is the half that is
usually skipped — reading feels like reconciling.

Before any work continues on an inherited item, the resuming session
regenerates the derived block and compares it against the one in the
handoff.

This is one command and a few seconds. It answers the only question
that matters at resumption: **has the tree moved since this was written?**

### What the comparison produces

| Result | Meaning | Action |

| Identical | Nothing changed | Proceed |

| Diverged | Stage, branch, gates or artifacts differ | Reconcile before proceeding; record what moved |

| Item closed | Someone finished it | Stop. Do not reopen on the strength of a handoff |

| Branch gone | Work was discarded or merged | Establish which before anything else |

| Cannot derive | The item, branch or artifacts are unreadable | Treat as diverged. Not as unchanged |

The last row matters and it is the one an implementation will get
wrong. An unreadable probe takes the conservative branch here as
everywhere else: a comparison that could not run has not established
that nothing changed.

### Divergence is normal

Most divergence is benign — the base moved, a dependency bumped, an
unrelated commit landed. The gate is not a wall, it is a reading. What
it prevents is the specific case where a session acts on a handoff
describing a state that no longer exists, which is where the expensive
mistakes live: fixing something already fixed, building on a reverted
decision, re-opening an item someone closed.

### The tree wins

Where the handoff and the derived state disagree, the derived state
is correct and the handoff is a historical record of a belief. This
needs saying because the handoff is more legible — it has explanations
and reasoning, and the derived block is a list of facts. Legibility is
not authority.

Record the disagreement rather than silently discarding the handoff.
A handoff that says `CAUSE-ESTABLISHED` where the artifact
says `CORRELATE-ONLY` is itself a finding: either the
artifact was downgraded after the handoff was written, or the handoff
overstated. Both are worth knowing, and the second is a provenance
failure the metrics should count.

### What resumption does not do

It does not re-verify the handoff's `[observed]` lines.
That would be re-running the previous session's work, which is the cost
this protocol exists to avoid. Observations are trusted as of their
timestamp; the gate checks state, not evidence.

The exception is `[assumed]`. A line the previous session
flagged as unchecked is unchecked, and if the current work rests on it,
checking it is part of the current work rather than an inheritance.

## Staleness

A handoff describes a tree at a moment. The tree moves. Nothing in
the document announces that it has stopped being accurate, and an
inaccurate handoff is more dangerous than no handoff, because it is read
with the same trust.

### Staleness is measured against the tree, not the clock

A handoff written an hour ago on a branch that has since been rebased
is stale. One written six weeks ago on an untouched module is not. Age
is a weak proxy; divergence is the real signal, and the resumption gate
already computes it.

So the rule is: **the derived block carries a fingerprint, and staleness is fingerprint mismatch.** Base commit, artifact
hashes, gate results, stage. The comparison in section 5 is the
staleness check — there is no second mechanism.

### Age still does one job

It bounds how long a handoff may be relied on when the fingerprint
cannot be computed. If the branch is gone, the item is closed, or the
derived block will not regenerate, the comparison returns nothing, and
then age is all you have:

| Age at resumption | Treatment |

| Fingerprint matches | Current, regardless of age |

| Fingerprint differs | Diverged — reconcile per section 5 |

| Cannot compute, under 7 days | Context, with the gap recorded |

| Cannot compute, over 7 days | Not usable. Re-derive from artifacts; read the handoff as history |

The last row is a real cost and it is the right one. A session that
cannot verify a month-old note and proceeds on it anyway is the
stale-authority failure with extra steps.

### The `[decided]` lines are the exception

A decision does not go stale the way a measurement does. *Fix at the detector, not at the gate* remains what was decided even if the
tree has moved underneath it — what may have changed is whether the
decision still makes sense, which is a judgment, not a fingerprint.

So `[decided]` lines survive staleness and carry forward.
If circumstances have changed enough to warrant reversing one, that is a
new decision, made by a person, recorded as such. An agent does not
quietly reverse an inherited `[decided]` line because the
situation looks different now — it raises it.

The other three tags do go stale. `[observed]` was true at
a timestamp. `[assumed]` was never checked.
`[proposed]` was never adopted and gets less likely to be
adopted the longer it sits.

### Handoffs are not accumulated

One handoff per item, replaced each time. A chain of six handoffs is
a document nobody reads to the bottom of, and the older entries are
exactly the ones most likely to be stale and most likely to be
quoted.

What carries forward into the replacement: every
`[decided]` line, and every `[observed]` line
whose evidence is still referenced. What drops: superseded observations,
`[proposed]` lines nobody picked up, `[assumed]`
lines that have since been checked (they become `[observed]`,
or they become nothing).

The previous handoff stays in git history. It is retrievable if
someone needs to reconstruct what was believed when — which is
occasionally the whole question, and is why replacement is not
deletion.

## No exemption by inheritance

The Descent Protocol closes the exemption that comes from
*discovering* work. This section closes the one that comes from
*inheriting* it, and they are the same failure arriving by a
different door.

**A prior session never satisfies a requirement for the current one.** Every gate that would apply to this work if it started
today applies to it now.

### The sentences that grant nothing

| What the handoff says | What it is not |

| "The previous session established the cause" | A diagnosis artifact |

| "Already reviewed by the last agent" | An independent review |

| "Tests were passing before the context ran out" | A recorded gate result |

| "We agreed the approach in the last session" | A `[decided]` line, unless it is tagged as one |

| "This was in scope for the original item" | A scope declaration |

| "Almost done, just needs the caller wiring" | Anything at all |

Each reads as a fact about work already done, and each is a sentence.
The artifacts either exist in the tree or they do not, and that question
has a mechanical answer the handoff cannot change.

### Why this is the likeliest failure in the protocol

The others are visible when they happen. This one is invisible
*and* it feels like diligence — a session that reads the handoff
carefully, believes it, and proceeds has done everything a conscientious
reader would do. The resulting commit looks properly grounded. The
grounding is a sentence.

It is also the failure with the longest tail. A diagnosis that was
never made cannot be refuted by the recurrence probe, because there is
no artifact to mark `REFUTED`. The fix lands, the symptom
returns, and the loop has no record of what to reopen.

### Partial work inherits nothing either

An item left at 80% does not arrive 80% governed. If the previous
session wrote the spec and the acceptance criterion, those artifacts
exist and the current session uses them — that is inheritance working
correctly, because the artifacts are real. If the previous session
*intended* to write them, the current session writes them.

The test is whether the thing exists in the tree, not whether someone
meant to make it exist. That is the same test everywhere in this stack,
and it is the reason section 4 derives state from artifacts rather than
from narrative.

### The one thing that does carry

`[decided]` lines. A decision made by a person is a
decision, and re-litigating it each session is its own kind of churn —
the mirror failure of inheriting an exemption.

So: decisions carry, evidence carries only as artifacts, and
permissions never carry. An agent that finds itself reasoning *the last session must have checked this* has found the exact sentence
this section exists to stop, and the correct response is to check
it.

## Enforcement, measurement, open decisions

### What binds where

| Control | Enforced by | Strength |

| Handoff exists at session end | Run wrapper writes it; a run that ends without one is flagged | Mechanical |

| Derived block is machine-written | Generator, not the agent | Mechanical |

| Every line tagged | Schema check on the handoff file | Mechanical |

| Resumption comparison ran | Chain record; resumption without it is flagged | Mechanical |

| No exemption by inheritance | Existing Root Cause and Correction Loop gates | Mechanical |

| Tags are honest | Nothing verifies that `[observed]` was observed | Behavioural |

| Open questions not acted on | Nothing refuses work that came from a handoff question | Behavioural |

Two behavioural rows, and they are the honest limits. An agent can
write `[observed]` over a belief, and the only check is that
an `[observed]` line must carry a command and an output —
which makes the lie effortful rather than impossible. And a session that
turns an inherited open question into work will be caught by the Descent
Protocol's depth and scope gates rather than by anything here, which is
adequate but indirect.

### The numbers

| Metric | Reading |

| Resumptions with a comparison run / resumptions | The headline. Below 1 means handoffs are being read, not reconciled |

| Divergence rate at resumption | High means work sits too long between sessions |

| Re-diagnosis rate | Diagnosis artifacts whose candidates duplicate a prior artifact for the same item. Direct measure of the failure this exists to stop |

| Tag distribution per agent | All `[observed]`, no `[assumed]`, is not a careful agent — it is an agent not using the vocabulary |

| `[proposed]` lines later cited as decisions | Provenance collapse, caught |

| Handoffs unusable at resumption (stale, uncomputable) | Work left too long, or artifacts not surviving |

| Items resumed by a different agent than wrote the handoff | The population this protocol is actually for |

**The suspicious zero: no `[assumed]` lines anywhere.** Every real session assumes things. A corpus with none
means the tag is unused and the other three are carrying beliefs they
should not be.

### Build order

| | Work | Note |

| 1 | Derived block generator | Everything depends on it, and alone it fixes silent incompleteness |

| 2 | Handoff schema and tag validation | Cheap; makes tagging real |

| 3 | Resumption comparison, one command | The other half of the protocol |

| 4 | Write-at-session-end in the run wrapper, including at compaction | |

| 5 | Replacement semantics: carry `[decided]`, drop the rest | |

| 6 | Re-diagnosis metric | The measurement that says whether any of this worked |

Step 1 alone is worth shipping before the rest. A generated state
block attached to every session end, with no tagging and no resumption
gate, already kills *built, tested* as a possible summary.

### Open decisions

**A — Who writes the handoff when a session ends badly?** A run killed at its wall-clock cap, or one that crashed,
writes nothing — and those are the sessions whose state is least
recoverable. Options: generate the derived block continuously so it
always exists, or accept that abnormal endings produce state-only
handoffs with no reasoning. I lean to the first; it costs a write per
stage event and it means the worst case still has something.

**B — Does the person's session need a handoff too?**
Everything here is written for agents, but you end sessions with context
in your head that nothing records, and the next agent inherits an item
you were thinking about. Probably yes, at a much lighter bar — the
`[decided]` lines are the part that matters, and they are the
part only you can write.

**C — Retention.** Handoffs live in git and accumulate.
A year of replaced handoffs for a long-running item is a lot of
superseded belief. Bound it, or accept the growth because it is small
text.

### What this protocol deliberately does not do

It carries knowledge **along an item**, not across the
system.

The autonomic computing literature is built around a shared knowledge
base — in the MAPE-K loop, Knowledge is a first-class component that all
four phases read and write, rather than a note passed between them.
Measured against that, this protocol is point-to-point: session A tells
session B about item X, and nothing connects item X to item Y.

What that misses is real. A cause established on one item is
rediscovered on another because nothing links them. A dead end probed in
March is probed again in September. The Correction Loop's signature
matching does some of this for *problems*; nothing does it for
*causes* or for what was learned along the way.

**Decided: not building a cross-item knowledge store now.** Two reasons. Per-item handoff plus signature matching
captures a large share of the value at a fraction of the cost, and
knowledge-graph projects have a long history of consuming more than they
return. The measurement in this section is what would justify revisiting
it: if the re-diagnosis rate falls for repeat work on the *same*
item and stays flat across *different* items, the gap is costing
something and a shared store becomes worth pricing.

Flagged for review rather than closed quietly, because it is the one
place this protocol set is structurally narrower than the prior art it
resembles.

### The honest limit

This protocol cannot make a handoff accurate. It makes the claims in
one checkable, separates what was decided from what was suggested, and
ensures nothing in it grants a permission. The reasoning in a handoff is
still the previous session's reasoning, with all the errors that
had.

What it removes is the specific class of churn where a session
re-derives what was already known, or proceeds on a foundation that was
a sentence. If the re-diagnosis rate does not fall after two cycles, the
tagging is ceremony and the derived block is doing all the work — in
which case keep the block and cut the rest.

## Complying with this protocol, before you write

> Run `node scripts/governance/obligations.mjs --files <what you are about to touch>` first. It returns
> what binds this change, deterministically and at no model cost, instead of asking you to carry the
> document. Being refused later is not compliance.

- Tag every claim paragraph `[decided]`, `[proposed]`, `[observed]` or `[assumed]` as you write it.
- Let the generator write the derived block; do not hand-edit it.
- A handoff describes work that may outlive its worktree. If the checkout is gone, reclaim before re-deriving: `node scripts/fleet/salvage-reclaim.mjs --branch <branch>`.

### Deviations, with reasons

**The fingerprint excludes head and working tree.** The document lists base commit, artifact hashes, gate results and stage. The first implementation also fingerprinted the head commit and the working-tree state, and writing a handoff then committing it moves HEAD and cleans the tree, so every handoff read as stale the moment it was committed. The signal would have become noise within a day. It now covers item, depth, parent, branch, base, diagnosis and verdict.

**Tags are per paragraph, not per line.** Enforced literally, a wrapped claim must be re-tagged mid-sentence. Tags that are noise get stripped.

**Only CLOSED blocks under `--gate`.** Divergence is the common case and usually benign, since main moves while a session works. A gate refusing every resume would be switched off within a week, and the CLOSED case would stop being caught with it.

**Derived fields are limited to what this repository can read.** Stage stream, capture store, chain record, CI gate results and run telemetry have no substrate yet; the generator writes UNREADABLE rather than omitting them.

**Scoped to the newest entry.** Every historical entry predates the protocol and would refuse.
